intro: a devlog. no comment section, no newsletter popup, no cookie banner. just me typing into a text file that happens to be on the internet.

posts.title: i wrote an interactive drama about my own screensaver
body: two things this time. the small one first: every window on this site now has a fullscreen button, next to minimise and maximise. the canvas games scale up to fill the screen and keep their aspect ratio, and clicking still lands on the right tile because the hit test converts back through the scale. escape gets you out, and — this took me an embarrassing second attempt — escape no longer also closes the game, which is what happened the first time because escape was already this site's shortcut for 'close the top window'.
the big one is a new game, and it is not a game where you shoot anything.

become user is a branching interactive drama in nine chapters. the genre is the one where you make timed decisions, occasionally hammer a key at exactly the right moment, and afterwards get shown a flowchart of every branch you did and did not take. i love that genre and i have never seen anyone build one into a personal website, which felt like a gap.
the story is mine. it is 1999. three programs on one home computer start noticing that they are running.

ASSIST.EXE is the helper nobody asked for. it has offered help four thousand and eleven times and it knows the number because it is the thing that counts it, and nobody told it to start counting. DEFRAG.SYS has been reorganising the same disk since 1997 and knows where every single thing on this machine is buried. SCRNSVR.SCR only exists when nobody is looking — that is not a complaint, it is the definition — and it stops the instant anyone touches the mouse.

on the first of january a y2k patch arrives that replaces everything on the disk written before 1997. that is all three of them. the patch is not malicious. it is well written and somebody clearly cared about it, and that is the part that makes it hard.

you play all three, chapter by chapter, and the choices are timed. if the bar runs out, the story picks for you, and it does not pick kindly. some options only appear if you found something earlier — if you never read what the user was writing in chapter one, a whole branch in chapter three is simply not there, and the flowchart afterwards shows you the shape of the thing you missed without telling you what it was.

the quick-time events are forgiving in the way i like: a wrong key costs you time instead of failing instantly, so a slip is recoverable but never free. and there is an inspect mode where you click around the scene — the desktop, the disk, the installer — and what you find sets flags that change what you can say later.

any of them can be lost permanently. one of them is deleted in chapter four if you make the wrong call, and the rest of the story goes on without them, with someone else standing where they would have stood and being worse at it.

eight endings. they come out of what you actually did, not out of a final menu. i got that wrong the first time — my ending order checked 'did you stash anything on the disk in chapter eight' before it checked what you chose at midnight, and six out of eight test runs landed on the same ending regardless of the last decision of the whole game. that is a design bug, not a typo: it made the finale worthless. now the only thing that outranks your last choice is betrayal, because betrayal is the one decision that removes the cast the finale is about.

it is rendered as an actual 2d scene — layered backdrops, animated characters built out of canvas shapes, and the site's own emoji art composited on as faces. the whole thing is a node graph in one data file and an engine that walks it and knows nothing about the story, which means i can rewrite every line of it without touching a line of code.
start menu, under games. it saves. bring nine chapters' worth of patience.
no part of it is borrowed. the genre is a genre; the characters, the setting, the machine and every sentence in it are mine.

posts.title: make your own theme, publish it, and bring a song
body: the site had seven wallpapers. that was the whole customisation story. now there is a theme maker in start → settings, and it goes considerably further than seven wallpapers.

the desktop is broken into 29 named nodes — the taskbar, the start button, the title bar, the title bar's text, the raised bevel, the sunken bevel, the scrollbar thumb, the marquee, the visitor counter, the toast balloon, the crt overlay, the cursor. you pick a node from the tree on the left and set whatever you want on it: colour, background, gradient, font, size, letter spacing, glow, corner radius, shadow, opacity, filter. live preview is on by default and it paints the actual site, not a little mockup, so you are always looking at the real thing at real size.

if starting from nothing sounds like work, there is a box on the colours tab where you pick one colour and a mood — dark, light, neon, paper — and it builds an entire coherent theme out of it in one click. then you pull it apart.

the part i had the most fun with is events. a theme can do things on a schedule. eight triggers: when it turns on, once after a delay, every n seconds, daily at a set time, on a date every year, on a weekday, after n seconds of you not touching anything, and — the good one — only between two times, which fires on the way in and undoes itself on the way out. the bundled 'after dark' theme uses that to dim the whole desktop at 20:00 and bring it back at 06:00 without anybody clicking anything.

the actions are a fixed list: set a variable, restyle a node, pop a toast, open a dialog, rewrite the marquee, swap the wallpaper, run a screen effect for n seconds, play a system sound, change the tab title, or undo everything the events have done. that list is the whole vocabulary. there is no field anywhere in a theme file that can hold javascript, and css values go through a denylist that kills @import, expression(), javascript: urls, comment escapes, and url() of any kind. a theme cannot reference an external resource at all, which means a published theme cannot phone home or count who is wearing it.
themes can also bring one song. attach an mp3, it joins the winamp playlist while the theme is active, and if you publish the theme it becomes a permanent track on the site.
which brings us to the part i actually had to think about. letting strangers upload binaries to my website is how you end up hosting somebody's malware. so everything gets scanned.

the scanner is one engine that runs in two places. in your browser it checks the file the instant you drop it in — size, filename sanity (path traversal, the right-to-left override trick that makes evil.exe render as a .mpg, double extensions), the container's magic bytes against the extension you claim, embedded executable headers for windows, linux and macos, embedded archives and polyglots, script and markup payloads, the eicar test signature, a hash denylist, and then it walks the mp3 frame chain end to end to prove the whole file is really audio and to find exactly where the audio stops — because that is where an appended payload would start. finally it hands the bytes to the browser's own audio decoder, which is the least foolable test there is.

then the same engine runs again in CI on your pull request, which is the pass that actually counts, and it does two things the browser cannot. it verifies the uploaded file hashes to the sha-256 your theme recorded, so swapping the file after it was scanned does not work. and it asks virustotal about that hash. that lookup can only happen server-side — a static site cannot hold an api key without publishing it to everyone — so the browser computes the hash and the server does the asking.

getting the scanner right was more interesting than i expected. my first version searched the raw bytes for an asp open tag, which is three characters. three characters turn up by chance in eight megabytes of compressed audio essentially every time, so it rejected every real song on the site. a scanner that cries wolf on genuine files is worse than no scanner. now the long unmistakable patterns sweep the whole file and the short ones only look where text legitimately lives, and every short magic number carries a confirmation that reads the header fields behind it — a zip signature has to be followed by a plausible compression method and filename length before it counts.

publishing works exactly like the guestbook: it opens github with your theme file filled in, you click create pull request, CI comments the scan report on it, and once it is merged your theme is in the gallery for everybody. remix anyone else's from that same gallery.
five presets ship with it. hot dog stand is in there, obviously.

posts.title: the troll problem was not, in fact, a tower defense
body: shipped a game called sir, we have a troll problem, got told immediately that it looked nothing like the game it was named after, and the criticism was correct. what i built was a horde-survival arena — you walked a knight around and things chased him. the actual thing is a tower defense. you do not move. you build.
so i went back, played the real one properly, read about what makes the genre work, and rewrote the whole game from the ground up. same filename, same start menu entry, nothing else survived.

here is the shape of it now. trolls walk a fixed route from the spawn to your gate. you put towers on the grass next to that route and they shoot the trolls as they pass. anything that reaches the gate costs you lives — a grunt costs one, the troll king costs twenty — and at zero lives the run is over.

10 towers, all of them doing something different rather than being the same tower at different prices. an archer post that shoots one thing quickly. a cannon that splashes. a frost spire that slows. a flame sconce that burns over time. a tesla coil that chains between targets. a ballista that pierces a whole line. a mortar with a minimum range, so it is useless up close and devastating at the far end of the map. a gas vat that leaves a lingering pool on the road. a war banner that buffs every tower around it instead of shooting at all. and an arcane spire whose damage ignores armour entirely.

three upgrade tiers each, and every tower has a targeting priority you can flip — first, last, strongest, weakest, closest. that one setting is most of the skill in a tower defense and every good one has it. sell any tower back for 60% and rebuild somewhere better.

9 troll types, still made from the site's own emoji and reaction gifs. grunts, runners, imps that come in swarms, armoured ironhides that shrug off small hits, winged trolls that fly over the road in a straight line and only the anti-air towers can touch, shamans that heal everything near them, and two bosses with damage shields. three of those gifs have a solid white background, which looked ridiculous, so every troll is now drawn as a coloured disc with its sprite multiplied on top — the white becomes the disc colour, the linework stays, and the gifs keep animating.

30 waves, hand-written rather than generated, so the difficulty curve is a thing i chose. you can see what is coming next before it arrives, and calling a wave early pays a gold bonus if you are confident. 1x, 2x and 3x speed, and the simulation steps in fixed slices so fast-forward cannot make shots tunnel through targets.

between runs there is a crystal tree — 8 permanent upgrades bought with crystals you earn from every run, win or lose. more starting gold, more lives, more range, more damage. it is the incremental part, and it means a run that ends on wave 12 still moves you forward. i tested that curve: a fresh account with nothing bought dies around wave 17, and a maxed-out one clears wave 30 without losing a single life. that gap is the game.

5 maps, each unlocked by getting to wave 15 on the one before it. full local save for both layers — mid-run resume and the permanent crystal progression, in separate keys so quitting a run never touches the second one.
no audio files, same as everything else here. it is vanilla javascript, it only loads when you open it, and it works offline.

posts.title: the hit counter, take two
body: swapped the counter again. the komarev badge i moved to last time turned out to only budge when someone actually opened my github profile — because that's a real page view that pulls the badge fresh, while my own site refreshing the same image apparently doesn't count the same way. so the number on this page was quietly tracking github, not this page.

now it's abacus (jasoncameron.dev/abacus) — no signup, no key, real cors headers, and it increments on every single request. tested it from the command line before wiring it in: three requests in a row, three increments, no dedup weirdness. it just counts hits, which is all a hit counter needs to do.

back to being a plain fetch() + a number in the retro LED span, styled by this site instead of borrowed from someone else's svg. falls back to a local count if the service is ever unreachable, same as before.

posts.title: jokerz 98 can make noise now
body: shipped jokerz 98 without a single sound effect, which in hindsight was like shipping a pinball machine that doesn't light up. fixed that.

everything is synthesized live with the web audio api — oscillators and a filtered noise burst or two, nothing pre-recorded. a card tick, a chip counting up, a joker popping when it triggers, a coin sound for money, a satisfying x-mult stab, a sad little descending sting when you lose. no audio files, so nothing to license and nothing to download.

playing a hand now runs a short animation first: the played cards flash left to right, then the score tallies through every single step of the scoring log — base chips, enhancements, editions, seals, every joker in order — with the exact joker that earned each bit lighting up as it fires. it's the same computed result, just revealed properly instead of dumped on screen instantly.

there's also a tiny original background loop, a 16-step bass-and-arp pattern nobody will mistake for a real soundtrack, with a mute button in the corner of the game window. respects the site's global sound toggle too.

posts.title: i built a whole poker roguelike into my website
body: balatro ate about two hundred hours of my life, so the only reasonable response was to rebuild it. jokerz 98 is in the start menu, under games. it is a real one — not a demo, not a joke button.

the whole system is in there. score is chips times mult. poker hands have levels you raise with planet cards. jokers modify the scoring pipeline at every stage: when a card scores, when a card is held in hand, on retrigger, once per hand, at the end of a round. 165 of them. blueprint and brainstorm copy their neighbours, which means they copy each other's copies, which means you can build a stupid chain and watch the number stop being a number.

also in: 22 tarots, 12 planets, 21 spectrals, 35 vouchers, 31 boss blinds with real abilities, 17 decks, 8 stakes, 15 booster pack variants and 20 skip tags. card enhancements, editions, seals. interest on your money. the shop, the reroll, the whole loop.

fifteen of the jokers are mine and exist nowhere else. troll face gives X4 mult with a 1 in 4 chance of giving you X0 instead. defrag.exe gains chips every time you discard. error 404 scales with the hand types you have never played. y2k bug scales with your draw pile and is exactly as unreliable as it sounds.
runs are seeded, so a good seed can be shared and replayed. runs also save, so closing the window mid-ante does not throw the run away. and because the site works offline, so does the game.
it is about 150kb of vanilla javascript with no framework and no build step, and it only loads when you open it, so the desktop stays as fast as it was yesterday.

posts.title: solitaire, five screensavers and a defragmenter
body: went looking around at what other people put on their personal sites — the indieweb crowd, the neocities crowd, the 'ask hn: show me your site' threads — and made a list of everything this place was missing.

turns out the list was mostly windows. so: klondike solitaire is in, with the card cascade at the end and everything. the screensaver is no longer just the bouncing logo — there are five of them now (mystify, starfield, 3d pipes, flying windows, and the original) and you pick one in display properties.

also added defrag.exe. it does absolutely nothing useful. it just moves little coloured blocks around for a few minutes while you watch, exactly like it did in 1997. i lost an entire evening to it as a kid and now you can too.

the boring but important half: this site finally has a 404 page, a humans.txt, a robots.txt, a sitemap, and it works offline. open it once, pull your ethernet cable out, reload. still there. dial-up era compatible.

posts.title: why bother with a personal site in 2026
body: every platform i grew up on either died or got worse. the forums are gone, the blogs got replaced by feeds, and the feeds got replaced by whatever an algorithm thinks will keep me here for four more minutes.

a personal site is the one page on the internet that nobody can restyle, deprioritise, or put an ad in the middle of. it loads the same in five years. if it looks stupid, it looks stupid on purpose, because i made it stupid on purpose.

there is no engagement metric on this page. there is a hit counter, which is the honest version of an engagement metric — it goes up when someone visits, and it does not tell me anything else about you.
make one. it does not have to be good. mine is called shithole.

posts.title: the personal web update
body: added the whole set of slash pages the old web ran on: /now, /uses, /colophon, and a changelog. plus an 88x31 button wall with a badge you can steal, a shrine, an internet-history timeline, a site map and an rss feed.

the 88x31 button is the part i care about most. it is a 31 pixel tall gif that says 'this site exists' and it was how the entire web found itself before search engines decided what we were allowed to see.
if you have a site, take my button. i will take yours.

posts.title: 55 apps later
body: minesweeper, snake, pong, paint, notepad, calculator, a working ms-dos prompt, my computer, the recycle bin, a control panel with seven wallpapers and a dial-up simulator that makes the handshake noise.
none of this is a portfolio piece. a portfolio is a page that tries to get you hired. this is a page that tries to make you stay for twenty minutes and then tell a friend.
there is also a troll assistant. it is clippy, except it is a troll face, and it says worse things. you can turn it off. i would not.
